content: Icodextrin, also known by its International Nonproprietary Name (INN) and United States Adopted Name (USAN), is a colloid osmotic agent derived from maltodextrin. It is utilized in the form of an aqueous solution for peritoneal dialysis under the trade name Extraneal. Additionally, it is employed after gynecological laparoscopic surgery to reduce post-surgical adhesions (fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs) under the trade name Adept. Icodextrin is a starch-derived, branched, water-soluble glucose polymer. Its structure is composed of α-(1→4) glycosidic bonds and less than 10% α-(1→6) glycosidic bonds, classifying it as a type of dextrin. The weight-average molecular weight of icodextrin ranges between 13,000 and 19,000 Daltons, while its number-average molecular weight is between 5,000 and 6,500 Daltons. The substance appears as a white to off-white solid, and its solution is clear and colorless to pale yellow. The osmotic activity of icodextrin allows the solution to remain within the peritoneal cavity for three to four days. This property helps separate tissues and reduces adhesion formation when fibrin is produced after surgery. In simpler terms, it prevents tissues from sticking together. When used for peritoneal dialysis, the icodextrin solution absorbs waste products from the blood and is subsequently removed from the peritoneal cavity along with the waste after a few hours. Icodextrin is not significantly metabolized within the peritoneal cavity. Instead, it is slowly absorbed into the bloodstream via lymphatic vessels, with approximately 40% absorbed after 12 hours. Once in the bloodstream, it is broken down into oligosaccharides by the enzyme alpha-amylase. In patients with normal kidney function, both icodextrin and its breakdown products are excreted through the kidneys via glomerular filtration. Icodextrin is contraindicated in patients with a known allergy to cornstarch, maltose, or isomaltose, as well as in those with glycogen storage disease or severe lactic acidosis. Adverse effects associated with icodextrin include peritonitis, respiratory infections, hypertension (high blood pressure), rashes, and headaches. Among these, only hypertension and rashes occur significantly more frequently compared to glucose-based solutions. The other adverse events are generally related to peritoneal dialysis itself rather than the use of icodextrin specifically. Icodextrin can interfere with certain blood glucose testing systems, leading to falsely elevated blood glucose readings. This occurs with tests that utilize glucose dehydrogenase pyrroloquinoline quinone (GDH-PQQ) or glucose-dye-oxidoreductase (GDO) methods. These inaccuracies can affect patients who have been treated with icodextrin.
